DISCOVERY DAY, NEWFOUNDLAND-ST. JOHN THE BAPTIST DAY, QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to note that today is the anniversary of the discovery of Newfoundland by Giovanni Caboto in 1497. While Newfoundland was not then a part of Canada, all of us are very happy in the knowledge that this important anniversary will mean so much to the people of Newfoundland as it certainly does to all the people from one end of Canada to the other. We congratulate in a special way our colleagues in this House from Newfoundland.

As hon. members already know, proceedings of the house will be suspended tomorrow in order that they may celebrate properly St. John the Baptist Day, the national holiday of French speaking Canadians.
On behalf of the government and, I am sure, of every member of this house, I want to extend our best wishes to all French speaking Canadians.
There is no need to recall the unique contribution made by the French element of this country to the planning and development of our institutions. It is also with the greatest
interest that we have observed, these last few years, the new upsurge, the new vitality of our French speaking compatriots. I have no doubt that in the years to come they will continue to leave their mark on the life of this country. This will only be possible if the mutual understanding and goodwill that made Canada a country in a class by itself continue to prevail.
I wish, therefore, that this 24th of June will not only be a day of celebration for a group that is proud of its traditions and customs, but an occasion for all Canadians to show those brotherly feelings and common interests which are the basis of our national unity.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: DISCOVERY DAY, NEWFOUNDLAND-ST. JOHN THE BAPTIST DAY, QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today is truly an auspicious day, as the Acting Prime Minister has mentioned. We wish to join with him in extending our congratulations and best wishes to the Members from Newfoundland. I can only say that Giovanni Caboto in the year 1497 was indeed lucky that he did not run into the hon. Member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
Speaking seriously for a moment, today is also an auspicious occasion in this House since I understand both the Acting Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport are celebrating their birthdays. We also extend to them our heartiest congratulations from this side of the House.
I join, Mr. Speaker, with the Acting Prime Minister in extending to our colleagues of the French language and to all French speaking Canadians our congratulations and best wishes on a day commemorating the existence and survival of their language and culture in America. It is a day significant for all French speaking Canadians, but equally significant for all Canadians.
Without the presence of French Canada there would be no Confederation and no Canada today. Confederation accorded constitutional recognition to the cultural and language rights of French Canada. In producing a new charter for Canada's second 100 years those rights must be recognized and emphasized. I believe, and the Conservative Party believes, in a Canada free, independent

June 23, 1965
St. John the Baptist Day and sovereign. The maintenance of that freedom, independence and sovereignty is based on the fundamental association of the Confederation partnership. I do not believe a strong and united Canada can be based on the principle of separation, whether modified, qualified or rendered in legislation. You cannot build unity on separation.
The challenge of our time lies in the adjustment of our national structure so as to provide full and complete participation by all Canadians in the partnership of Confederation. The celebration of St. John the Baptist Day should therefore be regarded as an occasion in which all Canadians can take pride, commemorating as it does the continuing contribution of French Canada within Confederation.

To all French Canadians on the occasion of St. John the Baptist Day, best wishes, greetings and heartiest congratulations.

We are also happy about the exploits of Giovanni Caboto, and extend our best wishes to the two ministers on their birthday.

maintopic: DISCOVERY DAY, NEWFOUNDLAND-ST. JOHN THE BAPTIST DAY, QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to join with the various groups in their words about the anniversary of the discovery of Newfoundland and the birthday of two ministers of the crown. I think we must also emphasize the work of the premier of Newfoundland who was instrumental in this province becoming part of Canada. I think we should wish a long life to Josephus Minuslignus, the premier of Newfoundland at this time.
On the occasion of the French Canadian feast day, I do not believe it would be appropriate for a French speaking Canadian to boast about his nation. On the other hand, I do want to point out that French Canadians

have always shown great loyalty and a good deal of civic spirit when they discovered the country and maintained in the province of Quebec the French language and culture in Canada.

maintopic: DISCOVERY DAY, NEWFOUNDLAND-ST. JOHN THE BAPTIST DAY, QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to offer my best wishes to the two ministers who are to-day celebrating their birthday. They were born under the same star, on the same day, have followed the same path and are still doing so. I trust these two gentlemen, who have won the esteem of all the members, will for a long time to come make available their long experience to those of us who are younger than they here in Parliament for I am convinced all have already benefited from their advice and friendship in the past. We are therefore happy to wish them the best, and we trust they will remain with us for a long time still, because we intend to stay here for a long while.
We also wish to take this opportunity to extend our very best wishes to the citizens of Newfoundland who are to-day celebrating an important anniversary.
It is tomorrow, June 24, that French Canadians will celebrate the feast day of their patron saint, St. John the Baptist. Parliament will take a holiday on the occasion of this feast day, that is, all members of the house, whether they come from Newfoundland or British Columbia, the Prairies, the Maritimes or Ontario.
We are happy to see the French fact in Canada being officially acknowledged by everyone in every Canadian province. We are happy to see that for the first time this year, this feast day will be celebrated by a holiday in the Canadian parliament. This will indicate the official recognition of the French fact and we are very glad about it.
I should like to take this opportunity to extend, on behalf of our leader, the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), and of the members of our group, our best wishes to all our French-Canadian fellow-countrymen on the occasion of this feast day.
As everybody knows, a rather tremendous development is taking place in French Canada and we hope it will go on in a quiet and peaceful atmosphere. We are convinced that even though this national holiday is celebrated in peace and quiet, this development will go on much longer and further for the benefit of all French Canadians in the country. subtopic: PORTS OF HALIFAX AND SAINT JOHN-LOSS OF TRAFFIC
PORTS OF HALIFAX AND SAINT JOHN-LOSS OF TRAFFIC
speechtext: Has the government any program or plan to compensate the ports of Halifax and Saint John for the loss of 200 thousand tons of traffic annually due to winter navigation on the St. Lawrence River, as stated in the Annual Report of the Maritimes Transportation Commission last week?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: PORTS OF HALIFAX AND SAINT JOHN-LOSS OF TRAFFIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the following information from the Atlantic Development Board in answer to this question.
The Board received a report last year from a firm of private consultants in which it was estimated that improved winter navigation on the St. Lawrence River was leading to a loss of roughly 200 thousand tons of traffic annually to the ports of Saint John and Halifax.
As part of its general program to improve the economic conditions of the two ports, the government has initiated a series of studies and has undertaken a number of substantive measures. Thus, the Atlantic Development Board has studies in progress on the possibilities of increasing grain shipments, on the
feasibility of establishing a container shipping service; and on the desirability of establishing an industrial park or parks in the Halifax-Dartmouth metropolitan area. The National Harbours Board has commissioned a series of studies on the origin and destination of traffic through the ports of Halifax and Saint John. Concretely, the Federal Government is aiding in the construction of the Saint John harbour bridge and the National Harbours Board is building a new marine leg for the more efficient handling of grain at Halifax.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to move the adjournment of the House in accordance with Standing Order No. 26 in order to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, namely the distressing situation that has developed in large parts of Quebec and Ontario due to the worst drought in living memory, the resulting great drop in farm production, the forced selling of livestock due to lack of fodder which will seriously depress the entire Canadian livestock market, the extremely grave effect on farm income, and the failure of the Government to take any initiative to determine an immediate course of action to deal with this critical emergency.

Yes, Mr. Speaker. I am sure that by this time many Members of the House of Commons realize the serious situation that exists throughout the Ottawa valley affecting the eastern part of Ontario and the western part of Quebec. Some counties are more seriously affected by the drought than others, but one fact that comes to our minds is that within the last few days farmers have found it necessary to dump a lot of

In four adjacent counties in the Ottawa valley there are 258,600 head of cattle, and the farmers find that their fodder is becoming exhausted and they have to do something in a hurry.
The effect on the cattle population is not the only serious aspect. In the Ottawa valley area and the western part of the Province of Quebec there are some of the finest farmers in Canada. They have spent a lifetime, as their fathers did before them, in building up foundation stock, and now they find they are going to have to market stock which it will take them a lifetime to replace. We also find that the production of fruit and vegetables in this area has been reduced to a trickle, resulting in increased costs to the consumer and leaving the producers with very little income.
I think this matter is very urgent, Mr. Speaker, and that we should take immediate steps to see if we can do something to relieve the situation and help the farmers of this area to lay plans for the future. In today's paper I note that the farmers of this area who have suffered from drought for the last two years have found it necessary to purchase large amounts of fodder and to borrow from banks, which is an added burden on top of the mortgage payments that some of them have to make. According to the press they are asking that a freeze be placed on their mortgage payments so they can re-establish themselves.
I ask, Mr. Speaker, that this matter be given serious consideration.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to support the adjournment motion, and make a few remarks on the question of urgency. It is well known that in the Ottawa valley there has been a lack of moisture not only this year but last year, and that the situation is now critical. The fact that it is raining this afternoon means very little, because it will take a great deal of rain to overcome the drought of the last two years.
The Provincial Government has asked the Federal Government for assistance, and I hope the Federal Government will accept this motion today on the basis of doing something about the situation immediately. We have had some indication from Quebec Members in recent weeks with regard to the situation in the Lake St. John area, where rainmakers produced rain steadily for 67 days. If rain is to come in time to help crops in the Ottawa valley this year, 10 days is too long to wait for this operation to start. It should be started tomorrow. The Government can provide this kind of assistance today, and should not wait for any other request from the Province of Ontario.
I am not completely convinced that this rainmaking operation works, but the situation in the Ottawa valley is so desperate that I think it should be tried. It is also very desperate in Timiskaming. While the farmers there were able to produce a great deal of

I draw Your Honour's attention to citation 100 of Beauchesne, paragraph 1, which says the adjournment must be for a purpose involving the administrative responsibility of the Government.
Now, unless we are going to change the pattern of providing assistance to farmers and others who are caught in disasters of this kind, we would have to wait on the initiative of the Province to set up some kind of emergency assistance program. The Province in turn would ask the Federal Government to pay a portion of the cost. This has always been done in the past. I recall in 1961, for example, when there was a widespread drought covering the three prairie provinces, assistance was given by the Federal Government. However, the program in each of the Provinces was initiated and administered by the local Provincial Government. The Federal Government was asked to pay a portion of the cost.
Then, Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw your attention to citation 100, paragraph 5, which says the adjournment of the House cannot be moved with reference to critical conditions prevailing generally in certain parts of the country. When it is a question of helping farmers, I think it behooves the House to take the necessary steps to solve their problems.
In our area of Saguenay-Lake St. John, as in the Abitibi area, the problem is altogether different. We have too much rain; here, there is not enough.
If we adjourn the business of the House, will this afternoon's discussion be useful? We must first determine whether it is a definite matter of urgent public importance and, second, whether the discussion can be useful.
Is there any urgency? Of course, there is. Since the first part of this session is to end today or Friday. But the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith) replies that we shall have full opportunity to discuss this matter during interim supply which may be called later today or on Friday. Now, I say to the President of the Privy Council that there are already several subjects he suggested we could take up during interim supply. There is the address submitted to the Queen of England by the province of Quebec, the Dorion report itself and the related leaks. Thus, there are several subjects to be discussed on interim supply, which means that there will be very little time left to discuss the serious problem of farmers who suffer

from drought. That would seem to confirm the urgency of a debate.
Now, the emergency of such a debate was proved a while ago. Moreover, another important aspect that needs consideration is that this would enable us to see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) in the house. It is obvious that requests on this matter must come from provincial governments and that the federal government takes appropriate action afterwards. This was not done but, on the other hand, the federal government has acted accordingly in other fields. The federal government could make decisions of its own as to the steps to be taken. The federal government, through the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), took quite drastic steps so that, after many discussions concerning rainmaking machines, they were taken out of the Saguenay-Lake St. John district which has now enjoyed ten days of fine weather.

For all those reasons, I think it would be useful to discuss the situation. I believe it is an urgent problem and it is urgent to discuss it because we are now in the dying days of this first part of the session. I think you should authorize such a debate. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank you for this opportunity. As already pointed out, this condition is one of the most serious that has occurred in this community during the last three quarters of a century.
The rainfall during the past crop season has been less than needed. There are grave circumstances facing the farmers. The area affected covers a great many different types of farmers. In Renfrew county it is mostly cattle raising and dairy farming and the dairy industry has certainly suffered.
One farmer told me yesterday that he was about to put in a milk cooler, but in view of present conditions he wondered if it would be necessary for him to instal it. Many of the farmers with dairy cattle in this area have already fed them what surplus feed was left from last year, and now find their pastures are becoming totally depleted. As I mentioned just a few minutes ago, at the time of the 1961 census the cattle population in the four counties adjacent to the Ottawa River totalled some 260,000 to 270,000. Many of them are dairy cattle. Many farmers have young stock coming along and, due to the shortage of pasture fodder, something will have to be done to alleviate their plight.
Farmers are taking unfinished feeders to the sales barns, which are overloaded, and according to one newspaper I notice that at Cobden and in Perth last week they continued selling cattle until the early hours of the morning.
Finished cattle at the present time are selling in the neighbourhood of 25 cents a pound. Considering the farmers' machinery costs and their capital investment, the return is not too much. According to reports, some of the cattle that have been dumped on the market because of lack of feed have been
June 23. 1363
2820	COMMONS
Drought Conditions in Ottawa Valley sold at ridiculously low prices, some even as low as 13 cents or 14 cents a pound.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
It is hardly necessary to point out that in such circumstances a farmer would certainly find himself in a drastic financial condition. It takes a number of years to lay the foundation for a herd. Cattle which he purchased two years ago most probably cost more than he can get for them at present, and this creates a drastic situation. During the last few years many young farmers have bought farms at reasonable prices and equipped them with stock and machinery. In 1963 and again in 1964 they found it necessary to buy feed for their stock. They had to borrow from the banks, and now they find themselves in a desperate situation, obliged to dispose of their stock at prices far below their value. Their output of dairy products is extremely limited; they are finding it necessary to buy meal, and cannot see their way clear to repay their loans to the bank, plus the interest on those loans. Yet if they fail they face the loss of their mortgages.
I do not think I need emphasize to you, Mr. Speaker, the great plight which the agricultural community is facing. Of course we hope to get rain immediately. That would help to bring on a second crop. It would help the grain. But whether we do or not, a degree of damage has already been done which cannot be repaired. Every one of these farmers will find himself in a difficult financial position this fall; he will find himself obliged to make severe readjustments in order to remain solvent.
This is why I have brought the present motion before the House. I want to see what can be done to establish confidence among these people, who laid the foundation for this great country of ours. I want to let them know that their representatives throughout Canada are thinking of them and are willing to give every assistance so as to tide them over this distressing situation. I believe others will wish to speak on this subject. This is a situation which I am sure we all regret. It is one which can be solved by co-operation and by putting our shoulders to the wheel.

speechtext:
Ottawa Valley members on both sides of the House have for some weeks been drawing this situation to the attention of the House. As time went by the problem facing our farmers became more critical.
It is true, as was stated by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith), that


according to strict constitutional procedure we have to await provincial initiative either from Ontario or from Quebec, which is also affected, before federal action can be undertaken in the normal course. But I do not think that because this has been the practice in the past a pattern need be set for the future. Some hon. Members may agree that in the past two, three or five years there has possibly been too great a tendency to await provincial action in circumstances such as these. From my own limited knowledge of constitutional law it seems that if anything is of sufficient moment to affect the national well-being there is constitutional authority for independent government action at the federal level whether or not it is a provincial matter in its original aspect.
This drought, I suggest, is of such consequence that it will affect the national wellbeing. It will affect food prices. Already there are cries of complaint from consumers. Food prices affect the nation as a whole and this being the case I suggest, with respect, that we at Federal level should consider action in this regard.
The Federal Department of Agriculture is convinced that the rain making program is a very long shot. I think today's newspapers say it is a 20 to 1 shot. The provincial Department of Agriculture considers the situation so grave that it is willing to spend $200,000 on a 20 to 1 shot. I know the Dominion Meteorologist doubts the validity of claims for rain making equipment. Well, I believe the hon. Member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) and some of his colleagues have been complaining that rain making equipment is only too effective. If there is any chance whatever, be it 20 to 1 or a 100 to 1, I hope the federal Department of Agriculture will see its way clear to participate in the rain making venture, in view of the severity of drought conditions in the Ottawa Valley.
This is one facet of the help we can give at federal level to farmers in their desperate plight at the present time. It is not merely a case of a drought this year only, nor is it a case of drought both this year and last year, as the hon. Member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) suggested. As far as the farmers of Renfrew County and the Ottawa Valley generally are concerned, this is the fourth year in which they have suffered severe loss through drought.
It seems to me we could take action at the federal level in connection with matters which are properly within the federal ambit, and that such action would be of considerable
June 23, 1965	COMMONS
help to the farmers in their present need. First, we could bring in moratorium legislation with respect to Farm Credit Corporation mortgages, and farm loans of all types, in any way supported by the federal Government. This would have application to loans under the machinery syndicates legislation, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation loans, and so on. This general area is within the federal ambit of jurisdiction. There should be a moratorium with respect to principal and interest on mortgages pending the alleviation of drought conditions.
Banking and interest are within the ambit of the federal authority. Most of the farmers affected have had to borrow heavily from the banks in order to carry on last year and this year. It is our duty to see to it that our farmers are not strangled out of existence, and we can help do this by relieving them of interest payments and payments on debts.
I am sure that in conjunction with the chartered banks we can make some arrangement whereby farmers will not be squeezed out of existence because this year they will not be able to pay interest on bank loans or make repayments of principal.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I also wish to point one other thing. I have suggested that the Federal Government should take the initiative as this is a national crisis. I have suggested that they should participate with the Province of Ontario in the rain making program, which quite properly was initiated by the province; that was the proper venue in which a measure such as this should be initiated. I have suggested that we should gladly, willingly and eagerly participate in this program irrespective of the technical opinion of the Dominion Meteorologist, because if there is any chance it is a chance worth taking. As I pointed out, there has been .42 of an inch of rain in the past month and this is the worse drought in 75 years. Last night some of us had the opportunity to meet with the members of the Farmers Union, who brought these critical difficulties very forcibly to our attention. In particular, Mr. Powers, the Vice President of the Union, pointed out the difficult situation in the Valley, as he comes from Beachburg in the Ottawa Valley, and I think he made a suggestion which it is my responsibility to draw as forcibly as I can to the attention of the House for the solution of this matter. As he pointed out, with which views I agree wholeheartedly, even if our rain making

Drought Conditions in Ottawa Valley program is successful at this time-which I hope we will participate in-and even if we do take these very proper measures to alleviate the farmer from the pressure of his current debts, as I suggested earlier, there is one further program that is most necessary and that we should initiate here.
As evidence of the situation that the hon. Member for Temiskaming (Mr. Peters) referred to earlier, namely the fact that last year there was a drought of catastrophic proportions in this area, we co-operated with the provincial Department of Agriculture of Ontario and instituted emergency measures by way of freight assistance in transporting cattle to market and by way of subsidy on hay imported into this area. This year there is no point in speaking of a subsidy with respect to the importation of hay, because the drought is so critical in other parts of the Province of Ontario-and I may say that this is not a unique area; in the great State of New York this year they are suffering a drought which I think is as critical and as serious as ours. Generally there just is no hay. Therefore a program of subsidizing the importation of hay into this area just is not feasible, but forage is very badly needed. As has been earlier pointed out, the farmer is in the position right now of having to sell at sacrifice prices cattle that should be sold much later, because he fears that even though he may be able to feed them right today, there will be no feed this fall with which to winter his cattle. Hay is not available. I am not a technical man but I certainly feel for the farmers in their desperate plight as sincerely and as deeply as I could if I had the necessary technical knowledge. There may be a good many solutions that are perfect and absolute here, but I know that with the technical abilities we have in the Department of Agriculture we can suggest a system of subsidized forage whereby we will be able to get the forage into this area on a basis of help and subsidy if need be. It cannot be hay; it must be some other type of forage, as hay is not available.
I think this is a desperate and dark hour in the lives of these people, most of whom have lived in this area of eastern Ontario for many generations. I do not think these are people who come running to Government every time something gets a little tough. I do not think they come to us on their knees, and they never will, because these are proud people. But I do suggest that if we have any function here whatsoever it surely is to see to it that we use every

Drought Conditions in Ottawa Valley measure and every available facet of governmental action that is available to us in order to alleviate this desperate situation of the farmers of eastern Ontario.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the House should be appreciative of the fact that the hon. Member for Lanark (Mr. Doucett) brought forward this motion so that this matter could be discussed. Before discussing it I would like to point out something that I think should be apparent to everyone. There is no Minister of Agriculture here. His Parliamentary Secretary is not here. That man who acts as the eastern representative of agriculture and makes so many silly statements, the Minister of Forestry is not here. The Acting Prime Minister is not here. The man that has been left to make this decision is a man who has aspirations for the Ontario leadership of the party and who appears to be given the leadership in this field. I think this is a disgrace.
I think there are solutions to this problem.
I was aware that it happened two years ago. The hon. Member representing the riding of Renfrew says it has been a factor for four years. Therefore the federal Department of Agriculture must have known that there was going to be a serious problem and these people should be here this afternoon to accept or reject some of the suggestions made by the Members. If this is not done, I am prepared to move an adjournment motion, because this discussion will serve no purpose at all. I think the farmers in the Renfrew area have the right to expect the federal Government to give some leadership to them, but there is in this House no one who can accept suggestions made by Members. I don't know what the country will think about it, but I am sure they are going to ask, "Is the Minister of Agriculture out selling the cattle that have been forced on to the market in the last few days, causing a surplus of cattle?" But the Minister is not here and is not responsible enough to have somebody here speaking for his department.
I think there is a federal responsibility in this matter and some Minister is going to have to get up and indicate what they are going to do about it. No wonder the Government wanted to oppose this motion this afternoon; they have no intention of even listening to us. The farmers deserve a better deal than that, because these farmers are faced with a serious plight. We will go on and discuss the problem, although it is not going


to do a damned bit of good, because there is nobody here to listen and this Government is not interested.
I look at the Renfrew Advance. They have pointed out a number of times in recent days how serious is this problem, and in the last issue of June 10 the headline is, "Drought ... Conditions worst in 25 years". This article goes on to say:
Area farmers are facing the worst drought to hit the Ottawa Valley in 25 years. Rains predicted for Monday evening turned out to be only scattered showers and many areas did not receive any moisture. Eganville was one area that had more rain than most places but even there the situation remains grave.
The Renfrew Mercury, another Ottawa Valley newspaper, headlines the story, "Shortage of rain may cause extensive losses in county". This article goes on to say:
Renfrew County farmers could be faced with massive crop failures this year if rain does not come within the next few days, it was learned this week.
This has been known for some time. I wonder whether the Member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene) and the Member for Renfrew North (Mr. Forgie) have not brought this matter to the attention of the Government, and this is why there is not someone here that can get up and say what the federal Government is prepared to do in this situation.

Mr. Speaker, I will accept the point of privilege made and will withdraw the inference which the hon. Member took out of my remarks, which inference I did not intend. The inference I intended to make is that they have not been able to persuade

the Government to take any action, and that no one here is prepared to take any action.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I note that the Acting Minister of Agriculture for eastern Canada is in the House. Perhaps he is in a position to say what the Federal Government will do. But I am not prepared to accept the remarks of the last speaker, who implied that if the Provincial Government is not willing to do anything, then the Federal Government is not in a position to do anything. That is not correct. We should be in a position to do something.
I do not think the Quebec Government arranged for those rain-makers in the St. Johns area. The Quebec Government had one heck of a time getting rid of them. The Federal Government had the right to continue this experiment by applying to the Government of Ontario to move the rain-makers to the Ottawa Valley, rather than to hire an outside firm from Colorado, not yesterday, as the hon. Member suggested, but three days ago at a cost of $100,000.
It is the responsibility of the Federal Government to take action in fields over which they have jurisdiction. The Federal Government could report to Parliament and ask it to consider the necessary steps. What is the point of our making a plea on behalf of these farmers if the Government Members intend to sit here until five o'clock, at which time the whole matter will drop. I do not think that is a fair attitude to take in relation to the plight of the farmers in this area.
We have also heard the suggestion that loans be made to the farmers in the area. I am not in favour of providing loans to the farmers in the Ottawa Valley, because they are now faced with a situation which, in my opinion, has continued into this year from last year. These farmers have spent all the money they have accumulated over the years as a result of this disastrous situation. These people have had to sell their beef cattle, which usually brings 25 cents a pound on the market, at a sacrifice price of an average of 14 cents a pound. This has also resulted in the loss of their potential breeding stock. These farmers will be in considerable difficulty for a considerable length of time before they build their herds back up to that position they were in before the disaster struck. By giving them loans we are only going to burden them again with payments that they will not be able to make.
We are not asking the Government to give the farmers loans. More drastic steps than

Drought Conditions in Ottawa Valley that are required to deal with this situation. Many things could be suggested in the way of helping these farmers. A great deal of the hay that was bought by the farmers in the Ottawa Valley last year came from my area, and much of that hay had been stored in barns for four, five and six years. Those supplies have been pretty well depleted. There are many areas in my part of the country which can carry 10,000 or 12,000 head of cattle. We might provide a solution to part of the problem if the Federal Government was prepared to facilitate the moving of the cattle.
The Federal Government now operates a community pasture in the Earlton area, and I am quite sure that the farmers who are not using a great deal of the grazing land in that area would be willing to make reasonable arrangements for the pasturing of a large part of the cattle of this area, provided the Federal Government would assist in moving them in. I do not know whether that would be a good idea or not, but it is a suggestion. Perhaps the agricultural representative in the Renfrew area could get together with the agricultural representative in my area and work out some arrangement. Perhaps some arrangements could be made to allow the farmers of the Ottawa Valley area to go into the area around Earlton to cut hay at a reasonable rate. Much of this hay was not cut last year and would not be cut this year under normal circumstances. I am sure there are several thousand acres of hay which will not be cut this year unless some such arrangements are made.
There are many things this Government could do which would not cost very much money, but if they have no intention of helping the farmers in these disastrous circumstances, then obviously we are wasting our time by continuing this discussion. If the general public in the Ottawa Valley find that this Government is as callous as it appears to be, they will not only look seriously at the grain and hay situation in the Renfrew area, but will look at the cost of fruits and vegetables right here in Ottawa in the Byward market. They will find that strawberries, which are not worth buying, will be selling at 75 cents a basket. They will wonder about this situation, and why the Federal Government did not examine it and do something about it.
This disaster will not only have an effect on the farmers of this area but also on the housewives who buy fruits and vegetables which will not be produced in any quantity this
June 23, 1965
2824	COMMON!
Drought Conditions in Ottawa Valley year. One of the members of the protective staff in this building spoke to me this morning and told me that a friend of his has five acres in strawberries but will not get enough this year to put into his freezer for his own home use, yet last year he found it difficult hiring enough help to pick the strawberries from that same five acres.
We have heard a lot of facetious remarks about rain making in Quebec. There was a group of individuals visiting this House yesterday attempting to make rain of a different kind. I am not prepared to say that one can make rain. I am not prepared to argue that you cannot seed clouds and create a certain amount of precipitation. I am certainly not in a position to tell you whether or not this method works on a grandiose scale and can produce rain for 67 consecutive days, just with a couple of machines in the countryside. On the other hand, I am not prepared to say that we should not investigate this and decide whether it does work.
If this situation continues in the Ottawa Valley, I am sure the ARDA program will have to be used in respect of almost all the farms in the Renfrew area. The wealth of these farmers has never been great enough to allow these farmers to survive two or three successive crop failures. If something is not done in respect of this disaster, these people will be moving off these farms into other areas next year. This is a critical situation and the federal Government has an obligation right now to do whatever it can to relieve the plight of these people, even if it is only through a pseudo-hypothetical means.
The hon. Member for Quebec suggested that no matter what is done about this problem, these farmers are not going to have a June hay crop; but as the hon. Member for Lanark (Mr. Doucett) stated, the farmers may be able to harvest a second crop this fall which will at least help solve the problem.
I do not know whether there is anything more I can add to this discussion. I am very sympathetic to the farmer, but I should like to warn both the farmers and the Members of this House not to consider adopting a system of providing loans to these farmers, because all that will do is bankrupt the farm communities in the Ottawa Valley. I am in complete agreement with what the hon. Member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene) stated, that there should be some kind of a moratorium in respect of federal loans in the area directly affected by this disaster, and that could include all farm loans, veterans 

farm loans, farm improvement loans and loans made under all federal Government acts. There should be a one or two year moratorium in respect of the payments. I caution the Members of this House again not to adopt a system of loans to these farmers in this disaster area. These farmers paid 65 cents for a bale of hay in the Renfrew area last year. They cannot be expected to pay that price again this year and repay their loans. They have had to sell their cattle at sacrifice prices, but I believe that is even better than paying 65 cents a bale for hay.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
The Federal Government should consider now the idea of moving equipment from other parts of Ontario to these grazing areas in order to cut this unused hay. That might be part of the solution to the problem. It might also consider assistance in respect of moving cattle to these areas. The effect of this disaster is not being felt only in the disaster area, but in other parts of the province. These people are selling their cattle at reduced prices and this is displacing the market in other areas. Surely some solution can be found to this problem. But I castigate the Government again for their lack of leadership and their lack of fortitude in looking for something they can do. It is all right for the hon. Member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) to say that the book does not allow us to do this, but with respect to other things we are able to look for some way to get around the book if we want to do so.
We have had a resolution before us in recent days containing 19 allied items. If the Government had stuck in another one providing for the payment of $10 million to the Renfrew farmers because of the crop failure,
I am sure everybody would have said that we could not turn it down and there would have been no argument that we could not do it. It all depends on whether we want to do it.
I suggest it is the Government's role to give leadership. I think the Cabinet will find that Members of the Opposition are very sympathetic with regard to the problem faced by the farmers of the Ottawa valley and will give favourable consideration to any reasonable proposition that the Government will put forward. I think the Government should stand up now and make some suggestions that will be advantageous to the farmers of this area.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot let this opportunity go by without saying at least a few words. Like other members, especially the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), I am not annoyed but disgusted with the lack of interest shown by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) for the farm problems of eastern Canada. As a matter of fact, he should have been in the house today, to listen to our suggestions and tell us about the decisions the government intends to take concerning this matter.
I see that the Minister of Forestry is back and will probably speak in the name of the Minister of Agriculture.
In my opinion, that is the least the government can offer to us and, at this stage I want to point out to the house that for two years now eastern Canadian farmers, particularly those of Quebec, have been asking for the appointment of a Minister of Agriculture for the east. But when you consider the low value of the present federal Minister of Agriculture and when you see that the Liberal government is not even able to find a good minister for the west, I think it is therefore useless to have another one for eastern Canada.
The Minister of Agriculture being absent from the house, I hope that the Minister of Forestry will take into consideration the recommendations that will be made this afternoon and that he will deal with them.
It was mentioned earlier that, two or three days ago, the Ontario government reached an agreement with some American firms to set up rain making machines, in order to

Drought Conditions in Ottawa Valley increase precipitation and check the drought now prevailing in this area.
Mr. Speaker, I must say immediately that I do not agree with that decision under the circumstances. In fact, last year, the Abitibi farmers sustained losses on account of those rain-making machines and it seems that when the mechanism of those machines is released, it is quite difficult to stop it. In fact, last autumn, throughout winter and even this spring, we had to fight against those infernal machines which did more harm than good. I know nothing of the experience and ability of the management of this American company but even if their machines can increase precipitation, they could be useful in a certain sector of the economy but harmful in others.
In my opinion, it would be much better to rely on Divine Providence and on nature as created to control the weather and the climate in our area.
It is undeniable, however, that some areas of the lower Ottawa valley are affected by drought, that they have suffered and are still suffering damages. I feel that the government should submit proposals this very day so as to solve this problem, not by offering loans to the farmers affected, but by providing them with grants in proportion to their present losses, because whether it be in the riding of Renfrew, in the Ottawa valley, in Quebec or elsewhere, farming is so uneconomic that the present difficulties resulting from weather conditions will surely cause great losses to the farmers.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to insist on one point. I said a few moments ago that the government should make proposals and take the initiative, if necessary, by inviting the ministers of Ontario and Quebec to meet with its representatives, not to study but to decide what help to give at this time.
Here I would like to recall the problem which arose last fall in the Abitibi, Temisca-mingue and Lake Saint John regions which were greatly affected not by drought but by over 67 days of rain in the Lake Saint John area and 69 in Abitibi, with distressing losses. In fact, losses exceeded $2 million in Abitibi only and I have here a newspaper article published in La Terre de Chez Nous, on February 24, 1965 which gives the results of a survey made in that connection. I shall read it for the information of the house and so that the Minister of Forestry may acquaint himself with it, in case he should not have already done so.

Here is what we read in La Terre de Chez Nous with regard to the inquiry conducted by the U.C.C.:
In order to inform the people as to the damages to farming due to excessive rainfall during the crop year 1964, the Amos federation of the U.C.C. has held a Gallup Poll with 1200 farmers scattered in all the Abitibi parishes. All types of farms have been reached.
The Gallup Poll concerned the main sectors of production, hay, oats, potatoes and dairy products. Even if it does not have a scientific value, it still reveals a situation which leads us to the conclusion that farming has incurred heavy losses in that area and that farmers are deeply affected economically.
The survey reveals total losses of $2 million for the area, or an average of $850 per farm. The hay crop was affected in a proportion of 35 per cent, oats, 40 per cent, and potatoes, 60 per cent. The dairy production decreased by 25 per cent and the purchase of feed cost $50,000 more than during a normal season. To that must be added $100,000 for the purchase of feed and hay for the winter feeding of livestock. It is obvious that farmers do not have the means to take on such losses when we know already they can hardly make both ends meet.
Well, Mr. Speaker, that is what happened last fall in the Abitibi area. A similar and perhaps more serious situation arose in the Lake St. John area.
But on several occasions since last fall members of the areas concerned and myself have requested assistance from the federal government, we have been told that the province should take the initiative.
The Minister of Agriculture of the province of Quebec was kind enough to send me last week some copies of the letters he exchanged with the federal Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays). But that correspondence is not complete, much to my regret. That is the reason why I placed a notice of motion for the production of papers today on the order paper of the house so as to complete this information.
I notice that the Minister of Agriculture of the province of Quebec made certain general requests in order to assist some farmers of that province. However, it is to be regretted that those requests contained nothing specific as to the damages resulting from the heavy rain last fall in the Abitibi and Lake St. John area. But the Minister of Agriculture none the less made general requests in connection with the damages due to hail and tornadoes. What was the answer of the federal Minister of Agriculture? He replied that he had indeed received these recommendations, and I quote an excerpt from his answer to Mr. Courcy:
You undoubtedly know my opinion on such problems. I believe that the best way to avoid such disasters is crop insurance.

That, Mr. Speaker, was the reply of the federal Minister of Agriculture to his Quebec counterpart. It meant: "Well, participate in the joint crop insurance program, and we will be able to help you out."
Several years ago other provinces, particularly in western Canada, suffered similar disasters. It does not seem that the federal government was so niggardly in helping them out. But as far as assistance to farmers is concerned, it is much more restricted. I do not know whether this is because the government or the Minister of Agriculture of the province of Quebec are not categorical or energetic enough in their claims, or whether they ask for this assistance rather as a favour, but in any event, that request has been submitted, suggestions have been made and the federal Minister of Agriculture has flatly refused to help the province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, I will not speak any longer on this matter, but I do want to urge the government not to consider the situation- everybody is aware of it and I think it has been outlined clearly enough in this house today-but to decide immediately how it will assist the farmers of the Ottawa valley and those who find it difficult to survive in the Abitibi-Temiscamingue area thus avoiding many farm bankruptcies. We must endeavour to enable all those farmers to continue producing what is necessary for everyone's survival, that of the Minister of Agriculture as well as everyone else's, for if the farmers stop producing for one reason or another, we shall all die from starvation.
Mr. Speaker, we do not want to see farmers in difficult situations due to similar catastro-phies, whether these stem from natural causes or not. But, at any rate, we must assist them in order to spare them serious difficulties, and to ensure first of all, that they can continue to grow, to expand and to improve their lot, and through a healthy agricultural economy ensure the welfare of the country as a whole.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I must thank the
Drought Conditions in Ottawa Valley Deputy Speaker as well as hon. members of this house for allowing today a debate on a subject of extreme urgency and even of national importance.
The hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Doucett), the mover of the motion I had the honour to support, has stated his views remarkably well and has described accurately the distressing situation in which the farmers of eastern Ontario and western Quebec find themselves at this time due to severe drought conditions which began nearly four years ago and which have grown worse in the last two years.
A while ago the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene) said that he had approached the government three weeks ago to discuss the problem.
It is surprising to note, that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) has been abroad for the past few days and that he is not here this afternoon. Equally disturbing is the fact that only yesterday, when asked in this house by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau)-who intended to participate in the discussion this afternoon but who could not be here on account of uncontrollable circumstances-if he could say whether there had been any consultations with the representatives of the province of Quebec on this matter of national urgency, the Minister of Forestry replied:
Not recently, as far as I know.
Then the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscaminque (Mr. Martineau) raised the question again, asking whether the federal government intended to take action on its own initiative with the provincial governments. And the Minister of Forestry answered:
The government cannot do that. The request must come from the provincial authorities.
That is why we discussed this question yesterday afternoon and decided to ask for the adjournment of the business of the house today to debate the problems facing farmers of eastern Ontario and western Quebec.
We have raised this question because we all recognize its urgency and importance, not only for the farmers who may be forced to give up their farms fairly soon if the federal and provincial governments do not take adequate steps, but also for the whole country, because it will affect all consumers, all farmers, as well as all regions of the country, more particularly the provinces of Ontario and Quebec.

Drought Conditions in Ottawa Valley
In my opinion, the federal Minister of Agriculture should immediately ask the Ministers of Agriculture of Quebec and Ontario to meet with farm organizations in order to discuss this tragic situation. Indeed, that should have been done several weeks ago.
In my opinion, when a provincial problem takes on a national character, the federal government or the federal minister concerned may ask his provincial counterparts to meet with farm organizations to discuss the situation and take the necessary measures. And that should be done immediately to find solutions and to stop farmers of eastern Ontario and western Quebec from panicking, as seems to be the case now.
It is imperative that, following this meeting which should be held this week, the federal government be in a position to announce immediately an assistance program and thereby, as I said a moment ago, dispel the panic which has apparently spread among farmers.
We have suggestions to make concerning this program of assistance. Some have proposed a moratorium on loans already granted. As for me, I do not believe the solution lies in lending the farmers money to pull them out of a hole or telling them that we are prepared to wait a year or two so they can repay their loans. If, for instance, a farmer has agreed to pay back the Farm Credit Corporation at the rate of $800 a year, and if such a payment is delayed, if the farmer is asked to make it next year or the year after when he is in a position to resume a normal life, when that time comes, he will have to make a double payment to the Farm Credit Corporation.
What we need and what I am asking the government to do, is to consider the possibility of amending the federal farm credit act so that this extension of one or two years, which would be granted to the farmers concerned, be added not after the first year the farmer will have received an income, but at the end of the refunding period of the federal farm credit.
We know that the federal farm credit act allows farmers to borrow money for 29 years and that, in order to change the regulations of the corporation, an amendment to the farm credit act would be needed. The Farm Credit Corporation can say to the farmer: "We are going to grant you a new loan, we will start anew and you will pay all the inspection costs and legal fees. That is what can happen at present. On the other hand, if the govem-


ment moved an amendment to the farm credit act with respect to disasters, then the Farm Credit Corporation could postpone until after the 29 year period the payments owing to them and which will have to be paid.
The same thing should apply to the farm improvement loans act; payments should be postponed seven or eight years, that is when the farmer is in a position to reimburse.
The government could also help with the interest on money borrowed last year or the year before. We know, for example, that farmers of the Ottawa district and western Quebec have borrowed $3,000 and will not be in a position to reimburse those loans before six years. They pay 6 per cent interest so that after six years, it will cost them 36 per cent more than they received; 36 per cent of the money they received will be paid as interest. It is therefore absolutely impossible for a farmer to make those payments in a time of crisis.
In addition, it was suggested earlier that cattle should be brought to areas where there are pastures. This made sense in western Canada, but I do not think it would be an ideal solution in our area, because if milk cows are transferred to pastures 200, 300 or 400 miles away, farmers would not be willing to travel to those distant places morning and night in order to milk their cows. Therefore I feel it is impossible to provide this form of assistance in the present case.
What the government should do is to tell the farmers under a specific program: We are going to help you, do not worry about hay or fodder for the winter season. The farmers could then change their farms entirely into pasture lands. If some farmers of the area had sown 30, 40 or 50 acres with oats and if they were sure of getting federal or provincial assistance, they would all be in a position to change those acreages into pastures for their cattle, since they would obtain in the fall the required fodder to feed their cattle during the winter.

Therefore, if our farmers in the area could turn whole farms or the acreage already seeded into grazing grounds, if the federal government and the provincial governments gave the guarantee needed for the winter months, we might be able to get to August, with some rain, because the grazing grounds would be better at such a time of the year.
The Minister of Agriculture will have to consider another factor when he meets the provincial ministers. There will certainly be a shortage of hay throughout Ontario and
June 23, 1965	COMMONS
Quebec next winter. That shortage will be acute enough to give rise to prohibitive prices and I cannot see a farmer buying a small bale of hay for 75c, 80c or even $1.
If the government asked at once the farmers of the Ontario and Quebec areas to cut as fodder everything which can be cut instead of letting oats get ripe, letting it come to term for feed grain, we could then avoid a shortage of hay in the provinces concerned. If later, this winter, the government accepted the Opposition's proposal to set up a feed grain agency for eastern Canada, we could compensate the loss of that grain by purchasing western feed grain which would replace the grain farmers have not been able to produce since they cut their oats and fodder acreage. This means that, in a few weeks, the government could assist the farmers from eastern Ontario and western Quebec who would like to feed their cattle on their farm, by subsidizing transportation and purchases. We know that feed grain can easily be harvested in the first week of August or towards the 15th of August and that it is excellent food for dairy and beef cattle, in short, for the whole livestock of those farmers.
We are making suggestions to the government; we are convinced that the situation has become too serious to ignore suggestions which could assist not only Ontario farmers but Quebec farmers as well.
Here are our suggestions: first, a meeting with provincial ministers concerned and farm organizations in order to establish an assistance program. Second, announce this assistance program as soon as possible to check the growing panic among the farmers concerned and the consumers and to show the farmers that they will get assistance from the federal and provincial governments.
Third, examine the question of federal farm credits or loans which farmers have obtained through banks and consider the possibility of extending after the period of 29 years repayment of loans granted by the Farm Credit Corporation and of extending by five, six or seven years the repayment period concerning loans granted under the farm improvements act.
Fourth, ask farmers in affected areas to use extensively their farm and even every bit of land on their farm as emergency grazing ground.
Fifth, ask Quebec and Ontario farmers to cut all the fodder they can in order to avoid a shortage next winter and use this fodder to help the farmers concerned; and say to Quebec and Ontario farmers: "We will have 22620-180

Those are a few suggestions which I think should be considered by the governments concerned; I have discussed them with several farmers of the area and they found them sound. They may not settle all problems but they will certainly help the farmers concerned.
Mr. Speaker, I may have taken a little more time than I thought I would, but since the house has agreed to discuss this matter until six o'clock, we will thus have the opportunity of hearing the Minister of Forestry tell us what the government intends to do. As regards this emergency, I should like to say that such a drought could have severe effects in the future. For instance, if the farmers sell their dairy cattle, the market will be congested. Those animals are unfinished, they are not good and are not ready to be sold. The price will be lower than the average and a shortage will thus be created in connection with the quality dairy cattle owned by many Ontario farmers. Next year, they will have to buy a complete stock and, on account of that, prices will be higher. That will not be in the interest of the farmers concerned nor in the interest of the other dairy producers in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I shall conclude my remarks by asking the government once more to do everything possible, not in 15 days, nor in three weeks, but right now, to settle this situation for the benefit of agriculture in Canada and more particularly in the Ottawa region.

I believe it is most obvious that the problem referred to at the beginning of this sitting is extremely serious, since the motion for adjournment of the business of the house was supported by all parties, including government members.
Mr. Speaker, we are aware that this is a serious and urgent problem, and before leaving, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) informed me of his concern on this matter. For my part, following the questions that were put to me yesterday afternoon in the house, I got in touch immediately this morning with the authorities of the Department of Agriculture to investigate the situation, and
June 23, 1965

Drought Conditions in Ottawa Valley I shall transmit later on to the house the information obtained.
Mr. Speaker, at this stage I would like to make a comment which seems to me of major importance. On two or three occasions this afternoon, reference was made to the absence of the Minister of Agriculture, when it is well known that he is away on an official mission to France and England where he has been attending a meeting of the OECD in Paris, and where he has met British cheese importers for the greatest benefit of agriculture, I am sure.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that more indulgence should be shown regarding the absence from the house of the Minister of Agriculture or other ministers who are away on official business for the good of their own departments or of the country as a whole. In fact, I was highly annoyed this afternoon by the remarks of a certain member who noted my absence from the house for about five minutes while I had gone to secure certain documents for this afternoon's debate. I myself am particularly aware of this, since I own about 200 acres of land under crop and probably 50 acres for grazing. For about a month or a month and a half, while we were short of water, I have been able to see the situation becoming more and more critical. This is nothing new for us, because it was the same thing last year. We did not have any water or hay and we had to get some from remote areas. I am surprised to hear most members, if not nearly all of them, say that it comes within the jurisdiction of provincial governments to initiate such solutions. They seem to forget completely section 95 of the British North America Act which provides that:
In each province the Legislature may make Laws in relation to Agriculture in the Province, and to Immigration into the Province; and it is hereby declared that the Parliament of Canada may from Time to Time make Laws in relation to Agriculture in all or any of the Provinces, and to Immigration into all or any of the Provinces; and any Law of the Legislature of a Province relative to Agriculture or to Immigration shall have effect in and for the Province as long and as far only as it is not repugnant to any Act of the Parliament of Canada.
This means that not only the federal government has a competing jurisdiction in farm matters, but that this jurisdiction is greater than that given to provincial legislatures. This jurisdiction is similar for immigration. Why always wait for the provinces to act, when the federal government has full and entire jurisdiction. Instead of infringing upon provincial jurisdiction in the matter of social security or any other field, why not assume the responsibilities conferred upon us by the British North America Act? Why not assume our responsibilities in the matter of farming? Why always shift our responsibilities to the prov-

The Province of Ontario has taken a narrow and restricted view of ARDA projects. They have related them to watersheds; without a watershed there can be no project. In the counties affected by this drought there are no community pastures. There are no deep wells, no public assistance arrangements for farmers.
In the thirties the drought in the West was followed by measures of great importance in reaching a long term solution of farmers' difficulties-for example, the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Under the constitutional arrangements which govern this country, the ARDA program was set up in such a way that grants were to be made by the federal Government. We have put a lot of new life into this program. I am proud of the enthusiasm the Minister has shown and the report he has submitted to this House. His addresses on the subject of rural poverty constitute a memorable series of speeches which I believe should be studied by scientists and sociologists across Canada.
The projects which have to go forward under ARDA arise at local municipal level and go to the provincial level. And it is there we find the dead hand; it is there we find the hand that kills, the hand that shows no initiative and no interest in a long term solution to the problems facing Eastern Ontario agriculture. The province is showing an interest in supporting a rain making project. The hon. Member for Acadia had something to say about projects of this kind. I do not know whether it works or not. Like my hon. friend from Renfrew South (Mr. Greene) I do not claim to be a farmer; but I am very much concerned about the farming communities I have the honour to represent in this House. I do know that unless some imagination is shown by the provincial authorities in the Province of Ontario, unless some interest is taken, unless they quit dragging their heels, we shall continue to suffer, in the absence of long term remedial measures. Those counties will suffer in the future as they are suffering now. The federal authorities are alert. They are concerned. Officials at federal level have made a number of technical suggestions and these are being reviewed at the present time. But we are not in a position where we can simply move on our own in disregard of the constitutional 22620-181
